Stuart Whitley ([[Chief Executive Officer|CEO]]) |products = [[Naval Vessels]] |revenue = $977 million |revenue_year = 2025 |operating_income = |income_year = |net_income = $16 million |net_income_year = 2025 |owner = [[Government of Australia]] |num_employees = 2,600 |num_employees_year = 2025 |divisions = |subsidiaries = |website = [https://www.asc.com.au www.asc.com.au] |footnotes = [https://www.asc.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/ASC-Annual-Report-2025_B5-WEB.pdf Annual report for year ended 30 June 2025] ASC Pty Ltd}} '''ASC Pty Ltd''', formerly the '''Australian Submarine Corporation''', is an Australian [[State-owned enterprise|government business enterprise]] involved with Australian naval shipbuilding, headquartered at the [[Osborne Naval Shipyard]] in [[South Australia]]. It is notable for building the {{sclass|Collins|submarine|1}}s and {{Sclass|Hobart|destroyer|1}}s for the [[Royal Australian Navy]]. ==History== [[File:Australian Submarine Corporation building.jpg|thumb|The ASC construction facility on the [[Port River]]]] [[File:HMAS Hobart under construction April 2015.JPG|thumb|[[HMAS Hobart (DDG 39)|HMAS ''Hobart'']] under construction by ASC at Osborne]] The Australian Submarine Corporation was formed when [[Kockums]] (designer of the {{sclass|Collins|submarine|1}}) formed a [[joint venture]] with [[CB&I|Chicago Bridge & Iron]], [[Wormald International]] and the [[Australian Industry Development Corporation]] to construct the six vessels.Yule & Woolner, ''The Collins Class Submarine Story'', pp. 76–80 The ASC construction facility was established on previously undeveloped land on the bank of the [[Port River]], at [[Osborne, South Australia]].Jones, in ''The Royal Australian Navy'', p. 244 Work on the site began on 29 June 1987, and it was opened in November 1989.Yule & Woolner, ''The Collins Class Submarine Story'', p. 127 South Australia had been selected as the site of the construction facility based on the proposed location of the facility and promises by the [[Government of South Australia|State Government]] to help minimise any problems caused by workers unions.Yule & Woolner, ''The Collins Class Submarine Story'', pgs 87-8, 128 By the end of 1990, Chicago Bridge & Iron and Wormald International had both sold their shares in ASC.Yule & Woolner, ''The Collins Class Submarine Story'', pp. 181–4 The shares were bought up by Kockums and the Australian Industry Development Corporation, with some of Kockums' shares then sold to [[James Hardie]] to maintain an Australian majority ownership of the company. On 5 April 2000, the shares in ASC held by Kockums were bought out and the company was [[nationalised]], despite a trend by the [[Howard government]] towards [[privatisation]] of government-owned companies.Yule & Woolner, ''The Collins Class Submarine Story'', p. 312 In 1991 the company had brought the insolvent Carrington Slipways in [[New South Wales]] to expand operations. {{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article122371006 |title=ASC buys Carrington Slipways |newspaper=[[Canberra Times]] |volume=65 |issue=20,549 |location=Australian Capital Territory, Australia |date=17 July 1991 |access-date=24 July 2020 |page=17 |via=National Library of Australia}} The company's name was changed from the Australian Submarine Corporation Pty Ltd to ASC Pty Ltd on 1 October 2004 to position it as a supplier of naval combat vessels in addition to being a specialist submarine supplier and maintainer.[http://abr.business.gov.au/SearchByAbnHistory.aspx?abn=64008605034 Historical details for ABN 64 008 605 034] Australian Business Register The name was specifically selected to reflect "the company’s future business and shipbuilding activities" and the establishment of their shipbuilding operations.{{Cite web |title=Our History - 2004 |url=https://www.asc.com.au/movies/2004/ |access-date=2022-12-17 |website=ASC Pty Ltd |language=en-AU}} On 31 May 2005, ASC was selected by the Australian Government as the preferred shipbuilder for RAN's Air Warfare Destroyers (AWDs) under the SEA 4000 acquisition contract, one the largest in Australian Defence history. The Australian Government granted first pass approval for the project and provided $455 million to ASC towards "the next phase of activities including further design work, workforce skilling, initial infrastructure investment and facilities construction."{{Cite web |date=2005-05-31 |title=ASC CHOSEN TO BUILD AIR WARFARE DESTROYERS |url=https://www.minister.defence.gov.au/Hilltpl.cfm?CurrentId=4890 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050702101609/http://www.minister.defence.gov.au/Hilltpl.cfm?CurrentId=4890 |archive-date=2005-07-02 |access-date=2022-12-17 |website=Defence Ministers & Parliamentary Secretary}} In October 2016, the Federal Government confirmed that ASC would be dissolved into three companies focused on different elements of current ASC works. One would be dedicated to the Air Warfare Destroyers, one to continued submarine sustainment and development and one to infrastructure development. Dissolution was expected to be complete by 2017.{{cite web |url=http://www.navy.gov.au/nuship-hobart-iii |access-date=6 October 2016 |title=NUSHIP ''Hobart'' (III) |publisher=[[Royal Australian Navy]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161006145752/http://www.navy.gov.au/nuship-hobart-iii |archive-date=6 October 2016 |url-status=dead}}[http://www.abc.net.au/news/2016-10-11/shipbuilder-asc-adelaide-to-be-split-into-three-companies/7921894 Federal government announces Adelaide based shipbuilder ASC to be split into three companies] ''[[ABC News (Australia)|ABC News]]'' 11 October 2016 Under agreements struck with the South Australian Government, the newly formed infrastructure owner and manager, Australian Naval Infrastructure Pty Ltd (ANI), completed the acquisition of the Techport business in November 2017, enabling it to effectively consolidate ownership of the newly named [[Osborne Naval Shipyard]] precinct. Assets acquired included the Common User Facility and all shipyard infrastructure.{{Cite web |last=Australian Naval Infrastructure Pty Ltd |date=2017–2018 |title=ANI Annual Report 2017-2018 |url=https://www.ani.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/ANI-AnnualReport-2017-18.pdf |website=ani.com.au/about-ani/}} On 27 July 2018, ASC delivered the second Air Warfare Destroyer, [[HMAS Brisbane (DDG 41)|HMAS'' Brisbane'']], to the [[Australian Defence Force]].{{Cite web |date=2018-07-27 |title=Second Air Warfare Destroyer delivered {{!}} Defence Ministers |url=http://www.minister.defence.gov.au/media-releases/2018-07-27/second-air-warfare-destroyer-delivered |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221217154936/https://www.minister.defence.gov.au/media-releases/2018-07-27/second-air-warfare-destroyer-delivered |archive-date=2022-12-17 |access-date=2022-12-18 |website=Defence Ministers - Defence Australia}} In December 2018, [[BAE Systems Maritime Australia|ASC Shipbuilding]] was structurally separated from ASC Pty Ltd, and acquired by [[BAE Systems Australia]]. In 2021, ASC Shipbuilding is officially re-named BAE Systems Australia Maritime.{{Cite web |date=2018 |title=Our History - 2018 |url=https://www.asc.com.au/movies/2018/ |access-date=2022-12-17 |website=ASC Pty Ltd |language=en-AU}}{{Cite web |title=Next-Generation Frigate Contract Awarded to ASC Shipbuilding Under BAE Australia|url=https://seapowermagazine.org/next-generation-frigate-contract-awarded-to-asc-shipbuilding-under-bae-australia/?print=print |access-date=2022-12-17 |website=[[Seapower (magazine)|Seapower]]}}{{Cite web |title=ASC Shipbuilding renamed as four companies tapped for Hunter class - Australian Defence Magazine |url=https://www.australiandefence.com.au/defence/sea/asc-shipbuilding-renamed-as-four-companies-tapped-for-hunter-class |url-status=live |access-date=2022-12-17 |website=Australian Defence Magazine |language=en}} In 2020, ASC and the [[CSIRO]] begin a two-year research collaboration looking to more efficiently repair precision submarine components by perfecting ‘cold spray’ additive manufacturing techniques.{{Cite web |date=2020 |title=Our History - 2020 |url=https://www.asc.com.au/movies/2020/ |access-date=2022-12-17 |website=ASC Pty Ltd |language=en-AU}} On 28 Feb 2020, ASC delivered the third and final Air Warfare Destroyer, [[HMAS Sydney (DDG 42)|HMAS ''Sydney'']], to the ADF, marking the end of the shipbuilding for the Air Warfare Destroyer project SEA 4000.{{Cite web |date=2022-12-18 |title=Shipbuilding continues in South Australia as final Air Warfare Destroyer delivered to Defence |url=https://www.minister.defence.gov.au/media-releases/2020-02-28/shipbuilding-continues-south-australia-final-air-warfare-destroyer-delivered-defence |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221217155920/https://www.minister.defence.gov.au/media-releases/2020-02-28/shipbuilding-continues-south-australia-final-air-warfare-destroyer-delivered-defence |archive-date=2022-12-17 |access-date=2022-12-18 |website=Defence Ministers}} In August 2022 ASC announced the opening of a new science and technology hub at [[Lot Fourteen]] in the [[Adelaide central business district]], where research projects in fields such as [[robotics]], [[artificial intelligence]] and [[machine learning]] would be undertaken.{{cite web | last=Willis | first=Belinda | title=ASC to open city science and tech base | website=[[InDaily]] | date=9 August 2022 | url=https://indaily.com.au/news/2022/08/09/asc-to-open-city-science-and-tech-base/ | access-date=9 August 2022}} ==Products== ASC rose to prominence in 1987 when it was contracted by the [[Government of Australia|Australian Government]] to design and manufacture a fleet of six {{sclass|Collins|submarine|1}}s for the [[Royal Australian Navy]] (RAN){{cite web |url=http://www.southaustralia.biz/CaseStudy/2007/08/04/ASC.aspx |title=ASC |date=August 2007 |publisher=Department of Trade and Economic Development |access-date=2008-08-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080723114115/http://www.southaustralia.biz/CaseStudy/2007/08/04/ASC.aspx |archive-date=23 July 2008 |url-status=dead}} in what was the largest defence contract ever signed in Australia. Although the submarine project was marred with difficulties throughout the 1990s, upon completion the ''Collins'' class were hailed as the most advanced diesel-electric submarines in the world. The difficulties continued, however, and the very expensive ''Collins''-class submarines have been plagued with troubles and controversy ever since.{{cite web|url=http://www.abc.net.au/am/content/2011/s3273293.htm |title=AM – UK expert to head submarine review 20/07/2011 |publisher=ABC News|date=20 July 2011 |access-date=2011-12-27}}{{cite web|url=http://www.aviationweek.com/aw/blogs/defense/index.jsp?plckController=Blog&plckScript=blogScript&plckElementId=blogDest&plckBlogPage=BlogViewPost&plckPostId=Blog%3A27ec4a53-dcc8-42d0-bd3a-01329aef79a7Post%3A33ac1cb3-9113-450c-9e21-79df838da52d |title=Ares Homepage |work=[[Aviation Week & Space Technology]]|access-date=2011-12-27}}{{cite news| url=http://www.theaustralian.com.au/news/nation/engine-problems-cripple-collins-class-submarines/story-e6frg6nf-1225789068076 | title=Engine problems cripple Collins-class submarines | date=21 October 2009 | work=[[The Australian]]}} ASC maintains the six ''Collins''-class submarines for their operational lifespans under a A$3.5 billion contract with RAN.Yule & Woolner, ''The Collins Class Submarine Story'', p. 315 To date, no other navy has expressed interest in buying a ''Collins''-class submarine. In 2005, the company was selected by the Australian Government, ahead of two other bidders, as the preferred shipbuilder for three new [[Aegis combat system|AEGIS]]-based [[Hobart-class destroyer|Australian air warfare destroyer]]s (AWD) under the [[Sea 4000 Project]]. The AWDs are scheduled to begin service in 2013.{{cite news|url=http://www.news.com.au/adelaidenow/story/0,22606,15464694-910,00.html |title=Australian Submarine Corporation wins navy ship tender |date=30 May 2005 |work=[[Adelaide Advertiser]]|access-date=2008-08-03 }}{{dead link|date=June 2016|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} ASC was also set to construct twelve [[Collins-class submarine replacement project|Shortfin Barracuda Block 1A]] diesel-electric submarines to replace the ''Collins''-class submarine currently in service with the Royal Australian Navy.{{Cite web|url=http://www.abc.net.au/news/2016-04-26/pm-announces-france-has-won-submarine-contract/7357462|title=Australian submarines to be built in Adelaide after French company DCNS wins $50b contract|last=Henderson|first=Anna|date=26 April 2016|website=ABC News|access-date=26 April 2016}} However, this was later cancelled in favour of a nuclear-powered attack submarine fleet. ASC also has contracts for production of [[Keka-class patrol boat|Keka-class coastal patrol boats]], produced in Hong Kong for use of Hong Kong maritime police, and the Series T.81 produced in Thailand for the use of the [[Royal Thai Navy]].{{cite web | title = Australian ship builder to build landing craft for Royal Thai Navy| url = http://www.pattayamail.com/298/business.htm#hd3| work = Pattaya Mail| access-date = 2 April 2011}} ==Possible privatisation== In February 2014, the [[National Commission of Audit]] recommended in its Phase One Report that the Commonwealth sell its interest in ASC.{{cite web|title=Market based solutions|url=http://www.ncoa.gov.au/report/phase-one/part-b/10-1-privatisations.html|publisher=[[National Commission of Audit]]|access-date=23 May extract: ASC Pty Ltd, formerly the Australian Submarine Corporation, is an Australian government business enterprise involved with Australian naval shipbuilding, headquartered at the Osborne Naval Shipyard in South Australia. It is notable for building the Collins-class submarines and Hobart-class destroyers for the Royal Australian Navy.
